The Nigerian Army has conducted a combined-arms military exercise in Bauchi State as part of efforts to strengthen its operational capacity, while seeking additional land from the state government for the establishment of a dedicated Armour Corps training ground. The Chief of Army Staff, Lt-Gen. Waidi Shaibu, made the request during a courtesy visit to Governor Bala Mohammed at the Government House, Bauchi, on Wednesday, a day after the Army conducted the fifth edition of Exercise MUGUN BUGU 2026 in Alkaleri Local Government Area. Shaibu said the proposed training facility had become necessary following the expansion of the Nigerian Army from eight to 12 divisions, which had increased the number of personnel requiring specialised and continuous training. He said, “Being an armour officer myself, I started my career here in Bauchi. The state is home to every armour officer, as many of us normally start our careers here before proceeding to other courses. “With the current expansion, many officers and soldiers have been coming to the corps for training, and the training continues throughout the year. “Being a training area generally, it also requires dedicated training grounds. We are therefore requesting a parcel of land that will be dedicated to the training of the Armour Corps.” Responding, Mohammed said the state government had approved the Army’s request, assuring that relevant military authorities would work with the government to identify a suitable location for the facility. The governor congratulated Shaibu on his appointment as Chief of Army Staff, describing his operational experience, particularly in the North-East theatre, as an important asset in tackling the country’s security challenges. He commended the Army and other security agencies for their sacrifices in maintaining peace and stability in Bauchi State. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. He said, “The relative peace and stability we enjoy today, which have enabled us to execute massive infrastructure development, agriculture and economic reforms, would not have been possible without the vigilance and synergy of the 33 Artillery Brigade, the Armour Corps and other security agencies.” The governor also commended President Bola Tinubu and the Army chief for approving the establishment of two additional Army battalions in the state. He said the deployment of personnel and logistics had enabled the new formations to become operational within a short period, adding that their presence would help address security vulnerabilities around border communities and forest corridors. However, Mohammed identified boundary disputes, kidnapping and illegal mining, particularly in border communities, as persistent security challenges requiring sustained collaboration among security agencies. He also pledged continued support for families of military personnel who died in the line of duty, saying their sacrifices deserved lasting recognition. Speaking at the grand finale, Shaibu said the exercise was designed to improve the Army’s training standards and operational capabilities in response to evolving security threats. He explained that the exercise provided an opportunity to assess command and control, tactical decision-making, teamwork and the coordinated deployment of different combat capabilities under realistic field conditions. According to him, the exercise was also intended to bridge the gap between institutional military training and the practical demands of operations. He said, “One of the most important outcomes expected from Exercise MUGUN BUGU is enhancing our capacity to conduct effective command and combined-arms operations. “In contemporary military operations, the coordinated employment of infantry, armour, artillery, signals and other combat and combat support capabilities, sustained by effective command arrangements, cannot be overemphasised.” The Army chief stressed that no single arm could independently provide all the capabilities required for successful military operations, noting that effective coordination among the different arms and services remained critical. He said lessons learnt from the exercise would strengthen interoperability, operational precision and the Army’s capacity to conduct coordinated and decisive operations. Also speaking, the former Chief of Army Staff and Special Guest of Honour, Lt. Gen. Faruk Yahaya (retd.), called for the integration of emerging technologies into the Army’s training programmes, operational doctrines and capability development. Yahaya said the changing security environment, characterised by terrorism, insurgency, banditry and emerging technological threats, required continuous improvements in military preparedness. He said, “The threat of any army lies not merely in the sophistication of its weapons, but especially in the training, resilience of its personnel and their determination to accomplish assigned missions.” The former Army chief urged the military leadership to prioritise technological innovation, improved training methods and stronger command and control systems. He also called for closer collaboration among the Army, Navy, Air Force and other security agencies through joint planning, intelligence sharing and coordinated operations. Yahaya urged the Army to critically assess the observations and lessons from the exercise to improve future training programmes and operational effectiveness. ENDS… Umar Sani
